summary: Cadillac's first Australian model is a 2.8-tonne dual-motor electric SUV that a permanent $32,000 cut has re-priced from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs, dropping it under the fuel-efficient LCT threshold and into FBT-exempt novated-lease territory. Reviewers agree on the hushed ride, the 530km WLTP range and the distinctive styling, but split hard on the cabin: CarExpert and carsales rate it genuinely luxurious, while Chasing Cars judges the materials and rear-seat packaging not good enough at any price. The unresolved risks are a three-outlet retail network across Australia and New Zealand, no tow rating at all, and the resale damage the cut inflicts on every car sold before it.
pros: The permanent cut from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs puts it under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold, so it now qualifies for the FBT exemption on a novated lease — it did not at launch.
530km WLTP from a 102kWh pack, and a 22.1kW three-phase AC onboard charger roughly double the 11kW most rivals fit, so a full charge on three-phase takes about five hours rather than overnight-plus.
793 litres behind the second row and 1,722 litres folded, against 526/1,536L in a Polestar 4 and 333L behind row two in a seven-seat Kia EV9.

Five years unlimited-kilometre warranty plus five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 12-month/12,000km intervals, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and a year of free public charging upgradable to three years or a 7kW home charger.

Genuinely quiet: active noise cancellation that pre-empts road impacts and a 19-speaker AKG Studio system with Dolby Atmos are what every Australian reviewer singles out, alongside 388kW/610Nm and 0-100km/h in 5.3 seconds.
cons: The $32,000 cut is a resale problem as much as a bargain — every Lyriq sold at $117,000 to $124,000 was re-based overnight to $90,000, and Cadillac does not report sales to VFACTS, so there is no local residual data to argue with.
Not rated to tow anything in Australia, where a Kia EV9 pulls 2,500kg braked and a Zeekr 7X 2,000kg.

Three retail outlets across Australia and New Zealand — the Rosebery Experience Centre in Sydney, a Port Melbourne test-drive venue and Auckland — with the promised Brisbane site still unopened, so servicing and panel repair mean a long trip for most buyers.
Super Cruise is not approved for Australian roads and the adaptive cruise ships without lane centring; there is also no head-up display and no native navigation at $90,000.

At 2,774kg and a claimed 22.5kWh/100km it is markedly thirstier than a Polestar 4 Dual Motor's 18.7kWh/100km, and Chasing Cars rates the rear seat's high floor and hard ISOFIX bracing covers as genuinely uncomfortable.
